supplemental_candidate_scan.text: The proposition applies in particular to Gauduchon surfaces. For a general Hermitian background, passing from smooth $u_j\in\HH_\omega$ to $u\in\PSH(X,\omega)$ requires control of the multipliers $\rho_{u_j}$ as well as the potentials. The supporting probabilities of \cref{chap:normalization} recover $\mu_u$ in the smooth case and give a conditional approximation theorem. General approximation independence and an adjoint identity for a weak linearization remain separate questions.
Whether positive $\mathcal V_\mu(\theta)$ forces bigness remains open here, even for a general nef background.

At exponent zero, uniqueness of the scalar leaves a separate question about the potential. Density degeneration affects comparison, while the positive-exponent family can impose a choice of critical solution. The restricted-density mass-concentration proof around \eqref{uni-eq:mixed-bounded} follows \cite[proof of Theorem~3.7 and Remark~3.8]{LPT20}. The exterior-ball proof of \eqref{uni-eq:normalzero} instead uses maximum propagation, following \cite[Proposition~2.4 and Theorem~2.5 in the cited preprint]{BG18}.

The analytic approximation results of \cref{sec:ideal-volume-approximation} combine the preceding volume continuity with the dyadic ideal-envelope limit. Rational mixing with a strict analytic potential removes the curvature error in any smooth big background. Two background comparisons then give the exact upper-volume excess in \eqref{eq:fixed-big-analytic-comparison}. Conversely, stretching and concavity of the ideal envelope make its fixed points closed under upper-volume comparison at positive lower volume. This proves the analytic criterion \cref{thm:analytic-model-volume-criterion} and the inherited Cauchy completeness there. The higher-dimensional zero-lower-volume boundary and ideal-theoretic positivity criteria in \cref{qu:hermitian-i-characterization} remain separate questions.

The incomplete example \cref{thm:incomplete-divisorial-metric} tests the big-class completeness question raised in \cite[Question~3.5]{DNGL26}. It does not settle the flow problem of \cite[Section~3.1]{DNGL26}, where the class, divisor and coefficients must come from specified flow data. Likewise, the normal-length examples have logarithmically weakened divisorial poles, not the nonintegrable pole with a smooth positive coefficient across the divisor required in that setting.

On singular spaces, regularity upstairs must be combined with descent. Dang \cite[Theorem B]{Dang26} proves continuity results for bounded solutions on resolutions under additional geometric and integrability hypotheses, notably the log terminal setting. This result does not cover arbitrary unibranch singularities in the problem posed in \cref{chap:research-program}. Pan \cite[Theorems A and A']{Pan25} constructs a Gauduchon metric on the regular locus of a compact reduced irreducible Hermitian space of dimension at least two. It is conformal and uniformly comparable to the given metric, and unique up to scale within that class. Control of conformal factors on a resolution is central to the construction. This external result motivates the singular trace questions in \cref{chap:research-program}.

For nonpositive $u\in\PSH(X,\omega)$ on this threefold, \cref{prop:general-damping-weights} gives finite measures for the critical weight $(1-u)^{-1}[\log(\mathrm{e}-u)]^{-a}$, $a>1$, with uniform tails and capacity continuity. The optimal damping rate remains undetermined here.

Changing the curve areas rescales the polar distances, and a zero area removes its metric coordinate. The comparisons in \cref{prop:weighted-product-metric-comparison} quantify this change even when the active coordinates differ. If the curve backgrounds converge uniformly to zero-area forms, the diameters vanish and the potentials converge in $L^1$, uniformly over the model tuples. Their limit still contains the normalized smooth potentials of the limiting backgrounds, by \cref{cor:arbitrary-product-zero-area-collapse}. Thus these loci describe concrete degenerations beyond the positive-volume theory. Extending the complete topology to general ordinary models, while retaining analytic closure and compatibility across backgrounds, remains open.

The three-dimensional torus in \cref{ex:gauduchon-persistence-torus} carries a Gauduchon form $\omega$ and a smooth potential $u\in\HH_\omega$ for which $\omega_u$ is not Gauduchon. Thus $u_t=u+t$ is a smooth Perron segment that is not stationary for the $L^2$ action. On a surface, the Gauduchon condition persists under potential perturbations by \cref{prop:gauduchon-potential-persistence}, but it does not cancel the first-derivative terms in \eqref{eq:hermitian-ltwo-geodesic}. Relating Perron interpolation to a complete metric on Hermitian singularity classes remains a separate problem.

For the data in \cref{qu:individual-equation-threshold}, \cref{cor:individual-positive-threshold-exponential} gives greatest exponential solutions, convergence of their scalars to $b_h(f)$ and total-variation convergence of their measures. Capacity convergence of the normalized potentials is the missing step. Under the root-tail condition of \cref{prop:root-uniform-tails}, \cref{prop:exponential-root-tail-modulus} quantifies the scalar and measure errors; a rate linear in the exponent needs additional control. Positivity and integrability of $f$ alone do not ensure a positive threshold. Exponential subsolutions when $b_h(f)=0$, and an extension of the density criterion to arbitrary non-pluripolar measures, are separate questions.

Thus singular-current attainment alone does not settle the equation. At zero lower mass, it is still unknown here whether root tails suffice, or even whether $\mathcal D_h^0=\mathcal D_h$. \Cref{prop:root-tail-continuity} characterizes the tail condition by continuity under uniformly bounded logarithmic perturbations tending to zero in measure. This is an order-interval statement, not unrestricted $L^1$ continuity of the threshold.

The cone must be specified in this question. Allowing additional directions can shorten path distances. The finite-dimensional metric calculations do not establish a distance on the entire infinite-dimensional quotient.

The comparison is compatible with changes of background as long as these controls persist. Smooth gauges preserve it after ordinary projection, by \cref{prop:model-comparison-gauge}. The fixed-potential limit in \cref{cor:ordinary-envelope-background-limit} retains lower volume and, at positive lower volume, the ordinary envelope. The uniform estimate \eqref{eq:vanishing-background-comparison} allows the curvature errors in analytic regularization to tend to zero, as in \cref{thm:analytic-approximation-curvature-error}. For two-sided perturbations, convex correction gives admissible transported models and a uniform comparison independent of the chosen strict reference at the level of limiting convergence. This yields the analytic criterion of \cref{thm:two-sided-model-transport,thm:two-sided-analytic-criterion}. These arguments do not cover loss of bigness or the higher-dimensional zero-volume boundary.

The quantified equality is stronger than realizing the divisorial part on one model. \Cref{cor:divisorial-current-ordinary-type} gives a canonical ordinary type for that part by combining its Gauduchon mass bound with a smooth current decomposition. It does not determine higher-codimensional trace data on further modifications. The exceptional-divisor formula in \cref{thm:trace-exceptional-difference} describes the discrepancy between the canonical types on two models, including a cocycle and approximation in linear mass. \Cref{ex:exceptional-trace-with-exact-potential} shows that a nonzero exceptional term is compatible with an exact trace potential: the term records information absent from the original model's divisorial part. Increasing the background ensures a competitor with controlled curvature; it does not automatically exclude additional divisorial orders. The curve-fibration proof reduces every further-model order to a one-variable multiplicity. Under the two mass properties, \cref{thm:decreasing-model-volume-continuity} controls Lelong numbers through the upper-volume deficit and a positive lower volume. Extending that control beyond these mass conditions remains the missing step.

For partial kernels, the general upper envelope bound is proved. A matching lower bound is available in the explicit regimes below, while the general problem remains open. \Cref{thm:fujiki-partial-kernel-limit} gives the full-dimensional kernel measure limit on a manifold with a K\"ahler modification and a positive-mass closed-curvature potential. The proof retains the relative canonical bundle: its Jacobian factor corrects both ideal integrability and the Hilbert norm. This geometric assumption implies BMP; the birational transformation identities themselves do not require it. On a holomorphic submersion with descended data, the source equilibrium theorem on the base gives a different exact limit upstairs. Write $m$ for the positive integer tensor power of the selecting line bundle on the Hopf $n$-fold. The Hopf example has growth degree $n-1$, and normalizing by $m^n$ would erase it. Adding the vertical Hermitian form recovers a nonzero measure, with the factor computed in \eqref{eq:hopf-partial-equilibrium}.

Locality of H\"older regularity and regularity of weighted extremals under a uniform density-in-capacity condition provide specific cases of the regularity problem; see \cref{sec:history-regularity}. These hypotheses do not cover every singular envelope or settle the lower-asymptotic problem above.

For the data of this problem, put $R_m=(q_m/(rm))^{1/(2r)}$. The range $q_m=o(m^{1/(2r+1)})$ is settled by \cref{thm:compact-growing-jets}: on every fixed multiple of the disc of radius $R_m$, the local weight error satisfies $mR_m^{2r+1}=q_mR_m/r=o(1)$. Its proof constructs global sections with the growing vanishing condition. Extending the range requires control of the weight remainder at the transition scale, rather than only a fixed-order kernel limit. Higher-dimensional analogues and transfer through Hermitian fibrations remain separate questions.

Upper and lower mass bounds are separate questions. On the standard Hopf threefold, smooth admissible potentials have unbounded masses, although their infimum is positive. Another compact threefold carries a balanced metric with finite upper mass and smooth admissible potentials whose masses tend to zero. These examples, in \cref{chap:hopf,sec:vanishing-lower-mass}, explain why a general Hermitian theory cannot assume either bound. The later mass-bound part develops the theory under explicit upper and lower bounds.

Analytic approximation remains possible in a positive Hermitian background. Correcting curvature errors keeps dyadic approximants in the original potential space, and their envelopes decrease to the ideal envelope. A uniform topology on ordinary classes then characterizes the analytic closure by equality of the two envelopes, even for classes with infinite-mass representatives (\cref{thm:ordinary-topology-analytic-closure}). This topology can identify distinct ordinary classes. It also changes under a smooth gauge change $\theta\mapsto\theta+\ddc\chi$ if the zero obstacle is kept fixed. Including all smooth obstacles restores invariance under this change, with the potential transformed by $u\mapsto u-\chi$. In a smooth big background with bounded mass and positive lower ideal volume, zero-obstacle equality implies equality for all smooth obstacles. The same implication holds without these volume conditions on curves and on the specified product constructions (\cref{prop:conditional-i-characterization,cor:curve-arbitrary-background-criterion,cor:general-auxiliary-all-obstacle-criterion}). The general zero-volume implication remains open.

The metric defined by a current on its regular set raises a further question. A H\"older potential gives local trace estimates and finite distance to a nonempty analytic boundary when the current is smooth and strictly positive off that boundary (\cref{thm:holder-current-distance}). A bounded potential alone gives no such conclusion. Radial examples have continuous minimal residuals and complete regular ends, already in closed K\"ahler classes. Here the integral controlling the potential differs from the integral controlling path length. These examples concern the strength of regularity assumptions rather than the loss of closedness.

In these examples one may write $f=F/R^2$ with $F=R^2f$ smooth and positive on $M$. This does not assert that $F$ extends smoothly and positively across $D$: the logarithmic factors make it tend to zero there. The examples concern integrable, logarithmically weakened divisorial poles. They do not settle completeness for a prescribed nonintegrable pole with a smooth positive coefficient across the divisor, or the flow compatibility question discussed in \cref{sec:history-completeness}.

The missing estimate in the converse direction is a lower bound along suitable threshold-minimizing sequences. Compactness of normalized potentials does not provide compactness of these Gauduchon metrics.

The auxiliary manifold may have unbounded mass; the proofs use no ambient mass bound. The complete metric and all-obstacle criterion concern this specified product locus. Extending the metric to unrestricted ordinary models remains open.

The cancellation $\mathrm{e}^{\rho}|\sigma|^{-2}=s$ leaves the deleted point at finite distance. Thus the exponential equation in a big class can have an incomplete metric even when its finite-energy solution is unique and has minimal singularities. Here the class is non-nef. Completeness under nefness or the additional compatibility conditions of a geometric flow remains a separate question; see \cref{sec:history-completeness}.

The distinction is caused by the order restriction on a smooth test: it cannot use a measurable increase of a density whose essential lower value is unchanged in every open set. Bounded measurable tests retain this information. The theorem concerns subsolution existence for individual $L^1$ densities. A characterization of exact normalized equations at $b_h(f)$, including their natural singularity class and finite-mass compactness, remains a separate problem.

The next estimate quantifies this scalar error when the density root is approximable by bounded roots. Whether an exponential subsolution exists when $b_h(f)=0$ is a separate question; \cref{thm:individual-exponential-subsolution} applies whenever such a subsolution is available.

The proof also gives a modulus on each fixed compact subset: combine its uniform smoothing error with the derivative bound $C/t$. A H\"older exponent would require a proved power bound on the curvature error modulus. For a smooth big background, \cref{lem:smooth-background-regularization-rate} supplies a linear curvature error by refining the classical expansion. Together with stability above a strict barrier, it gives local H\"older continuity even for minimal-singularity solutions in \cref{thm:big-minimal-holder}. Neither argument asserts continuity across the pole set.

The relevant test metrics can be normalized by $\int_Xh\wedge\gamma^{n-1}=1$. A positive lower bound for $D_\mu(\gamma)$ along one threshold-minimizing sequence would finish the second step. The Gauduchon equation can change the volume density while retaining an Aeppli class. Since $\alpha$ is closed, it also retains the numerator paired against $\alpha$. The missing estimate is control of the trace normalization and determinant denominator after that change. Merely prescribing a volume density does not give this estimate.

The first assertion is a case of the volume-to-bigness question. Once bigness of $\theta_\tau$ is known, the parabolic theorem recorded in \cref{sec:history-geometry} supplies convergence as currents and smooth local convergence off $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta_\tau)$, by parabolic estimates. Combined with nefness and the qualitative null-locus theorem, this identifies the analytic exceptional set. Thus the missing step in this route is the proposed numerical criterion for bigness. The local envelope continuity and homogeneous replacement arguments of \cref{thm:big-continuous-envelope-contact} supply an elliptic foundation away from a strict barrier's poles; they are not a reconstruction of those parabolic estimates.

Completeness requires an additional metric estimate. In \cref{thm:incomplete-divisorial-metric}, the unique finite-energy solution of a divisorial exponential equation in a big closed class is incomplete on every nonempty connected open subset of its ample locus. Its minimal divisorial singularity cancels the prescribed pole. This resolves the unrestricted big-class completeness question negatively; it does not decide completeness under nefness or under the compatibility conditions of the geometric smoothing problem discussed in \cref{sec:history-completeness}. In particular it does not settle \cref{qu:chern-ricci-gaud-singularities}, whose limiting background is nef.

The regularity of the residual also matters. By \cref{thm:holder-current-distance}, a H\"older residual on a compact manifold gives finite distance to its analytic singular set wherever it defines a smooth positive metric off that set. Continuity alone does not suffice: the prescribed radial densities in \cref{thm:radial-endpoints} have bounded continuous minimal remainders and complete regular ends when $n<d\leq2n$. These examples concern their specified densities; they do not establish the flow compatibility in \cref{qu:chern-ricci-gaud-singularities}.

The singularity and divisorial constructions in the book become relevant at this stage: they record how much positivity can be spent on imposed poles, while the residual Gauduchon volume stays finite. They do not yet give the moving intersection product or the birational volume formula of the closed theory. Recovering such geometric information is a further objective, with the finite-divisor and Hopf calculations serving as explicit tests.

The estimates for separated potentials do not answer this question. The known collapse on $\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1$ leaves that class of potentials. On the K3 example every compact curve is vertical, so averaging such curves cannot supply the horizontal directions used in \cref{lem:lower-mass-curve-average}. A proof of collapse would need a different construction, while positive lower mass would require a bound for all admissible potentials or all normalized Gauduchon tests.

The same tail estimate gives a uniform exponential-damping modulus and scalar error bounds in \cref{prop:exponential-root-tail-modulus}. It does not, by itself, give capacity convergence of equation potentials. When lower mass vanishes, equality of $\mathcal D_h^0$ and $\mathcal D_h$ remains a separate question.
The smaller-background condition is an additional hypothesis. Its validity for an arbitrary threshold solution in this semipositive dual setting is not established here.

To identify the whole normalized limit for these symmetric data, we now use the radial equation. It determines the invariant solution even among bounded potentials whose differentiability is not known beforehand.

These conditions concern the maximal global coefficient. Realizing divisorial components from the resulting annihilating currents remains open; a threshold within a prescribed singularity type is a different problem.

For arbitrary changes of background, inclusion of the competitor families gives an order on the envelopes. Equality of their ordinary types would require a reverse singularity bound. For curve fibrations, the fixed divisorial potential in \cref{thm:curve-fibration-exact-trace} supplies this bound in every sufficiently large background.

Here $g:\Omega\to\Omega$ is the indicated automorphism, and $\langle g\rangle$ is the cyclic group generated by it. Its action is free. Indeed, equality of two projective points in one orbit would require the same scalar to be $1$ on the nonzero $z$ block and $q^k$ on the nonzero $w$ block. Thus $g^k$ has a fixed point only for $k=0$.

The example also makes the endpoint in \cref{thm:gaud-determinant-endpoint} fail for the full family of normalized Gauduchon currents: its supremum of $L^{3/2}$ determinant-density norms is infinite, although every subcritical $L^q$ norm, $1<q<3/2$, remains uniformly bounded by \cref{thm:gaud-determinant-subcritical}. An endpoint estimate restricted to the maximizing currents that represent adjoint measures remains a separate question.

For continuous $F$, uniqueness of the supporting probability is equivalent to all maximizing currents having the same normalized determinant-weighted measure. This is weaker than uniqueness of the current. Representing such a current as a conformal multiple of a weak power $\omega_u^{n-1}$ is a further question, discussed in \cref{sec:history-gaud-volume}; the construction here uses its coefficient measures directly.
